title: Simply The Best
body:
I’ve found that the best apps are those that appear simple on the surface and become more advanced when you need other features. 

Obsidian has absolutely mastered this concept of visible simplicity along with hidden complexity. 

You can use it as just a basic notes app with folder and tags. It will do everything Notes or Bear or any other notetaking app can do on the surface. It’s minimalist and beautiful. Not cluttered by insane UI like Evernote.

But you can also create advanced bases and templates that allow automatic categorization and interlinking of notes so you can always find old notes again. It’s built on a fundamental idea that your notes are just a collection of markdown text files in a folder. So the app is incredibly fast, future proof, and light weight. No custom files, and no bloat. Like others have mentioned, there are community plugins that are fantastic. Anything you can do in Evernote and Notion, you can do in Obsidian but way way better. And for a non-native app, it runs incredibly smoothly on iOS.

title: Lost Many Stories
body:
I heard many good things about this app for story planning and writing, so I decided to give it a try so I can properly organize my markdown files and write stories. Only had it for a day and never have I been more horrified. The last thing I expected was for Obsidian to completely make my markdown files disappear from my external drive for all my fanfiction works. Thankfully my original fiction remained untouched. That would have been worse if it did. All the worldbuilding, notes, research, and chapters I wrote for those fanfics are gone. Like they never existed. Did the usual troubleshooting, but nothing brought it back. I was lucky I was able to file recover in one of my cloud drives to get the files I have lost. I’m terrified of losing my works and don’t want a repeat of this experience, so I’m moving over to a different app. It’s a huge deal breaker if my works are lost this easily with Obsidian. Not only that, I’m not able to access my external drive on the app, which is another huge deal breaker as cross platform is a must have and I don’t want to be paying a subscription just to be able to cloud sync + cross platform for all my creative writing works when I can simply just one time purchase external storage then plug in then write. I have no plans of using Obsidian again. Don’t recommend for serious writing. Only if you’re working on one device and are using cloud sync, that is. If you want to write seriously and/or rather use an external storage for creative writing, I suggest finding a different app.

Overall, hugely disappointed since I heard so much good things about this app for notetaking, planning, and creative writing. So, I had expectations. Unfortunate that Obsidian didn’t meet them.

Edit: I decided to give it a chance again, but this time through Obsidian Sync. It was a bit unintuitive to figure out how to set it up, but figured it out eventually. However, as much as Obsidian is great on computer, the app had so much delay when it comes to writing on mobile. Which is unfortunate because cross platform is a must for me and compared to other apps and softwares I have used in the past like iA Writer, Scrivener, LibreOffice, Ulysses, Bear, etc., the delay when you press onto a new line then try to type since it’s trying to sync is noticeable. The plugins also act funky on mobile. Ended up refunding it the same day I got Obsidian Sync and just sticking with the current app I use to write. Because of the delay issues, plugins acting funky, and the fact that Obsidian does mess with my files, I’m still keeping it at my current rating. Obsidian is only good on computer and if you choose work locally only without cross platforming and syncing. As much as I did enjoy what Obsidian offers, it just isn’t optimized well enough and I don’t really trust that it’ll prevent my drafts, research, notes, and ideas + concepts from disappearing like it never existed or corrupting, randomly duplicating files or folders, and reliably syncing to the cloud. Otherwise, I still highly recommend looking at a different app if you need that cross platform, no typing delay, and apps that have some built-in features that plugins from Obsidian offers. Like I said, if you only work locally, not cross-platform, and not cloud sync, Obsidian is great on computer.
developer_response: Thanks for your feedback. Sorry you had such a harrowing experience. Background sync is on the roadmap. It should greatly improve the kind of workflow you described.

title: Love it
body:
As a writer, I have tried a wide range of writing apps—from the built-in iPhone Notes and Pages with its bare-bones functionality to more specialized tools like Scrivener. But as of 2026, I can say with confidence that Obsidian is better than all the others.

Yes, it is very geeky. Yes, the developers tend to overthink the application, which makes Obsidian feel overloaded in places. But—and this is important—none of that is mandatory. You can use Obsidian as a simple note-taking app that gives you plenty of freedom to organize your workspace and workflows to suit your needs, and only later, gradually, explore its more advanced features if and when you want to.

In short, whatever tasks you may need a note-taking app for, Obsidian is definitely worth trying.

title: An extensible, flexible tool for power users
body:
Obsidian is a highly flexible app that gives users many affordances with regard to customizing both the appearance and behavior of the app through its extensive list of community plugins and themes. With over 2,000 plugins, you can do almost anything you want with Obsidian—task management, writing, brainstorming, research, etc.

The app itself is also local-first and used Markdown, meaning your notes are stored on your device where Obsidian and third parties can't snoop on your notes. Markdown is a plaintext format that is commonly used in everything from messaging apps, documentation sites, blog posts, and more. Because your notes are in a common, plaintext format stored on your device, you'll be able to access and edit them even if Obsidian disappears.

Obsidian itself is developed by a small team of just seven engineers as of January 2026, and they don't rely on VC funding at all. They update the app frequently—my favorite changes as of late have been Bases, the latest mobile app design overhauls, and widgets for mobile. (Psst, if an Obsidian developer is reading this, support for push notifications on mobile would be a godsend for any task management workflows since it'll enable reminders that work without me having to use an external app like TaskForge.)

Now for as much as I praise Obsidian, there are aspects about it that will put some people off. First and foremost, syncing your notes across your devices will require you to pay for a subscription service. Furthermore, the extensibility of the app has made it daunting for new users, as the app (by default) does not come with many of the features that users have come to expect from using other note-taking apps; Obsidian can be tailored to most workflows, but that takes a lot of trial and error to reach.

Essentially, if you're someone who doesn't mind needing to customize your app to get it working, Obsidian provides plenty of features and affordances for you. Beyond that, there are other note-taking apps out there that might suit your needs better, like Joplin, Bear, or Notesnook.

title: I Want to Love This App
body:
Maybe it’s just the way our brains age, but I’m a 40yo well-educated professional in technology and education and this app is incredibly intimidating. If you don’t already work in markdown this may not be the best place to start. Trouble is that the other 5 star reviews are spot on, I see the tremendous value and I’m certain that Obsidian could easily take over as my singular app to handle the vast majority of my work that has otherwise been  spread across a stupid  number of apps. But where do you even start? Tried to lean on the native support resources, but the presentation and vocabulary require either a foundation of understanding, or a companion resource to understand the guide. There’s got to be a way to configure this program in a “simple mode” that intuitively unfolds further functionality as needed rather than exposing the entire spread of tools expecting new users to know enough to pare back those features that may not be necessary early on (backlinks!?!).

Additionally, many of the plugins are clearly written by coders and developers for other coders and developers to understand. Additionally I’m not a programmer much of the learning curve can become cumbersome and fosters a sense of futility. 

Good example; what’s the virtue in obsidian creating daily notes for dates where no notes were created? 

The slash command is handy, however I often don’t know the difference between similar concepts such as bookmarks vs links vs backlinks etc, and furthermore what practical purpose these seemingly different features enable. 

Just my two cents but if anyone has a killer way to learn this tool I’m all ears. 

If you are on the fence, I say try it out, hopefully it makes more logical sense to you!

title: Feature Suggestions to Enhance Obsidian
body:
Dear Obsidian Team,

First, I want to sincerely thank you for developing Obsidian—it’s truly an amazing tool for organizing knowledge and linking ideas in an intelligent and structured way. Its attractive design and dark theme make it enjoyable to use and inspire daily creativity.

I have some suggestions that could make Obsidian even more versatile and user-friendly:
	1.	Add support for attaching images and videos directly within notes.
	2.	Add support for voice notes, enabling users to quickly capture their thoughts.
	3.	Enhance support for reminders, audio, images, sketches, exporting to PDF, dark mode, and easy navigation with sections and categories.
	4.	Include the ability to lock notes or the app with a password or biometric authentication for sensitive information.
	5.	Keep the app completely free and fully offline.

I know that Obsidian wasn’t originally designed for this side of use, but believe me, you will receive a lot of support from the community if these features are implemented.

Believe me, my friends, implementing these features will elevate Obsidian to a whole new level and make it even more engaging and widely used.

Thank you again for your efforts. I am excited to see the future of Obsidian with these enhancements.

Sincerely,
[wolf slasher]

title: More than just a note-taking app
body:
Obsidian is a great note-taking app. Using markdown, it’s easy to write and format notes, link between them, and port them between platforms and even open them in other apps.

With Obsidian, there is no concern about your notes being lost when the developer sunsets their app, raises the price, or sells out to a Microsoft. 

But where Obsidian really shines is its extensible architecture and large library of plugins. It’s easy to add features, adjust how Obsidian looks, and integrate with other apps. This makes it possible to set up Obsidian as a the core of your daily organizing routine. Both a personal nerve center and a second brain.

It’s not perfect. It opens a little more slowly than simpler note-taking apps, especially when loaded up with a bunch of plugins. It may occasionally crash (in particular, some community-made plugins are not very stable). Syncing between devices can be a little finicky if you don’t use Obsidian’s native sync service. 

Overall, though, Obsidian is amazing and has won a place on my “must-have” app list.
